L107: Parliamentary elections were held in 【39†Iceland】 in 1844.^{【40†[1]】} They were the first elections in the country's history.^{【41†[2]】}
L108: ## Electoral system
L109: 
L110: [【42†edit】]
L111: 
L112: The 【43†Althing】 was composed of 26 members, twenty of which were elected and six of which were appointed by the monarch. The twenty members were elected in single-member constituencies by plurality voting. Each voter had two votes, with the runner-up becoming the MP's deputy.^{【44†[3]】} Voting was restricted to male property owners over the age of 25.^{【41†[2]】}
L113: The constituencies were the 【45†counties of Iceland】 in addition to 【46†Reykjavík】, the country's capital and only 【47†market town】 at the time.

L103: Parliamentary elections were held in 【36†Iceland】 in the autumn of 1874.^{【37†[1]】} The elections were the first after the introduction of a 【38†new constitution】, which granted legislative and financial powers to the 【39†Althing】 and increased the number of members from 27 to 36.^{【40†[2]】}^{【41†[3]】}
L104: ## Electoral system
L105: 
L106: [【42†edit】]
L107: The 30 elected members of the 【39†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by a three-round system; in the first two rounds, a candidate receiving a majority of the vote was elected; if seats were still unfilled after the second round, a third round was held using 【43†first-past-the-post voting】.^{【41†[3]】} Voting took place at a single polling place in each constituency and was done publicly.^{【41†[3]】} A further six members were appointed to the upper house by the 【44†Danish monarch】.^{【40†[2]】}
L108: Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over who were not in receipt of poor relief and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or meeting various tax criteria (for farmers, paying more than the minimum tax; for burghers or fishermen, paying eight 【45†króna】 of local taxes; for property owners, paying twelve 【45†króna】 of local property taxes).^{【40†[2]】} This limited the number of voters to 6,183 from a population of 70,595.^{【46†[4]】}
L109: ## Results
L110: 
L111: [【47†edit】]
L112: 
L113: 1,211 of the 6,183 registered voters participated in the elections.^{【46†[4]】} All candidates were independents, as there were no political parties in Iceland at the time.^{【41†[3]】}

L104: Parliamentary elections were held in 【36†Iceland】 in June 1886.^{【37†[1]】}
L105: ## Electoral system
L106: 
L107: [【38†edit】]
L108: The 30 elected members of the 【39†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by a three-round system; in the first two rounds, a candidate receiving a majority of the vote was elected; if seats were still unfilled after the second round, a third round was held using 【40†first-past-the-post voting】.^{【41†[2]】} Voting took place at a single polling place in each constituency and was done publicly.^{【41†[2]】} A further six members were appointed to the upper house by the 【42†Danish monarch】.^{【43†[3]】}
L109: Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over who were not in receipt of poor relief and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or meeting various tax criteria (for farmers, paying more than the minimum tax; for burghers or fishermen, paying eight 【44†króna】 of local taxes; for property owners, paying twelve 【44†króna】 of local property taxes).^{【43†[3]】} This limited the number of voters to 6,648 from a population of 72,449.^{【45†[4]】}
L110: ## Results
L111: 
L112: [【46†edit】]
L113: 
L114: 2,036 of the 6,648 registered voters participated in the elections.^{【45†[4]】} All candidates were independents, as there were no political parties in Iceland at the time.^{【41†[2]】}

L104: Parliamentary elections were held in 【36†Iceland】 in June 1894.^{【37†[1]】}
L105: ## Electoral system
L106: 
L107: [【38†edit】]
L108: The 30 elected members of the 【39†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by a three-round system; in the first two rounds, a candidate receiving a majority of the vote was elected; if seats were still unfilled after the second round, a third round was held using 【40†first-past-the-post voting】.^{【41†[2]】} Voting took place at a single polling place in each constituency and was done publicly.^{【41†[2]】} A further six members were appointed to the upper house by the 【42†Danish monarch】.^{【43†[3]】}
L109: Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over who were not in receipt of poor relief and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or meeting various tax criteria (for farmers, paying more than the minimum tax; for burghers or fishermen, paying eight 【44†króna】 of local taxes; for property owners, paying twelve 【44†króna】 of local property taxes).^{【43†[3]】} This limited the number of voters to 6,733 from a population of 73,230.^{【45†[4]】}
L110: ## Results
L111: 
L112: [【46†edit】]
L113: 
L114: 1,779 of the 6,733 registered voters participated in the elections.^{【45†[4]】} All candidates were independents, as there were no political parties in Iceland at the time.^{【41†[2]】}

L196: Parliamentary elections were held in 【79†Iceland】 in June 1902.[ 1 ]
L197: ## Electoral system
L198: 
L199: [【80†edit】]
L200: The 30 elected members of the 【43†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by a three-round system; in the first two rounds, a candidate receiving a majority of the vote was elected; if seats were still unfilled after the second round, a third round was held using 【81†first-past-the-post voting】.[ 2 ] Voting took place at a single polling place in each constituency and was done publicly.[ 2 ] A further six members were appointed to the upper house by the 【82†Danish monarch】.[ 3 ]
L201: Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over who were not in receipt of poor relief and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or meeting various tax criteria (for farmers, paying more than the minimum tax; for burghers or fishermen, paying eight 【83†króna】 of local taxes; for property owners, paying twelve 【83†króna】 of local property taxes).[ 3 ] This limited the number of voters to 7,539 from a population of 79,181.[ 4 ]
L202: ## Results

L192: Parliamentary elections were held in 【79†Iceland】 in June 1903.[1]
L193: ## Electoral system
L194: 
L195: [【80†edit】]
L196: The 30 elected members of the 【43†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by a three-round system; in the first two rounds, a candidate receiving a majority of the vote was elected; if seats were still unfilled after the second round, a third round was held using 【81†first-past-the-post voting】.[2] Voting took place at a single polling place in each constituency and was done publicly.[2] A further six members were appointed to the upper house by the 【82†Danish monarch】.[3]
L197: Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over who were not in receipt of poor relief and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or meeting various tax criteria (for farmers, paying more than the minimum tax; for burghers or fishermen, paying eight 【83†króna】 of local taxes; for property owners, paying twelve 【83†króna】 of local property taxes).[3] This limited the number of voters to 7,786 from a population of 79,632.[4]
L198: ## Results
L199: 
L200: [【84†edit】]
L201: 
L202: 4,155 of the 7,786 registered voters participated in the elections.[4] The result was a victory for the 【85†Home Rule Party】.[5]

L194: Parliamentary elections were held in 【79†Iceland】 on 10 September 1908, alongside a 【80†referendum on prohibition】.[ 1 ]
L195: ## Background
L196: 
L197: [【81†edit】]
L198: 
L199: The 【43†Althing】 was dissolved by King 【82†Frederik VIII】 in the early spring in order to elect a new parliament that would vote on a draft status law that would define the position of Iceland in the Danish realm.[ 2 ] The election campaign was one of the acrimonious in Icelandic political history due to the controversial nature of the draft.[ 2 ] The opposition was led by 【83†Skúli Thoroddsen】, a member of the 【84†Independence Party】.[ 3 ]
L200: ## Electoral system
L201: 
L202: [【85†edit】]
L203: The 36 members of the Althing were elected from a mix of single-member and two-member constituencies.[ 4 ] The elections were the first to take place since changes to the electoral system in 1904; they were the first to be held using the 【86†secret ballot】,[ 5 ] and also saw the three-round 【87†majoritarian system】 replaced by 【88†plurality voting】 as multiple rounds of voting on the same day were no longer possible.[ 4 ] The tax qualification for voting was also reduced, increasing the proportion of people able to vote to around 14% of the population,[ 4 ] up from 7,786 in 【89†1903】 to 11,726.[ 6 ]
L204: ## Results
L205: 
L206: [【90†edit】]
L207: 
L208: Candidates opposed to the draft law won a landslide majority, whilst voter turnout was 72.4%, nearly 20% more than the 1903 elections.[ 6 ] As a result, the law was voted down in 1909,[ 2 ] resulting in the resignation of 【91†Minister for Iceland】 【92†Hannes Hafstein】.[ 3 ]

L191: Parliamentary elections were held in 【77†Iceland】 on 28 October 1911.[ 1 ]
L192: ## Electoral system
L193: 
L194: [【78†edit】]
L195: The 30 elected members of the 【41†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by 【79†first-past-the-post voting】, with six members appointed to the upper house by the 【80†Danish monarch】.[ 2 ][ 3 ] Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, holding a medical (or similar) degree, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or paying tax of at least four 【81†króna】 (or for farmers, any level of tax), and who were not in receipt of poor relief.[ 3 ]
L196: ## Results
L197: 
L198: [【82†edit】]
L199: 
L200: 10,303 of the 13,136 registered voters participated in the elections.[ 4 ]

L191: Parliamentary elections were held in 【77†Iceland】 on 10 September 1914.[ 1 ] They were the last parliamentary elections in which only men could vote.[ 1 ]
L192: ## Electoral system
L193: 
L194: [【78†edit】]
L195: The 30 elected members of the 【41†Althing】 were elected from single or double member constituencies by 【79†first-past-the-post voting】, with six members appointed to the upper house by the 【80†Danish monarch】.[ 2 ][ 3 ] Suffrage was limited to men aged 25 or over and who met one of several set requirements including being a civil servant, holding a medical (or similar) degree, being a graduate of a university or seminary, or paying tax of at least four 【81†króna】 (or for farmers, any level of tax), and who were not in receipt of poor relief.[ 3 ]
L196: ## Results
L197: 
L198: [【82†edit】]
L199: 
L200: 7,475 of the 13,400 registered voters participated in the elections.[ 4 ]

L223: Parliamentary elections were held in 【87†Iceland】 on 15 November 1919.[ 1 ] Voters elected all 26 seats in the Lower House of the 【40†Althing】 and eight of the fourteen seats in Upper House.[ 2 ] The 【41†Home Rule Party】 remained the largest party in the Lower House, winning 10 of the 26 seats.

L213: Elections to the Upper House of the 【36†Althing】 were held in 【84†Iceland】 on 8 July 1922.[ 1 ] Following reforms in 1915, the six seats in the Upper House appointed by the monarch were abolished, and replaced with six elected seats.[ 2 ] The seats were elected by 【85†proportional representation】 at the national level, using the 【86†D'Hondt method】.[ 2 ] The remaining eight seats were elected along with the Lower House.

L133: Parliamentary elections were held in 【53†Iceland】 on 27 October 1923.^{【54†[1]】} Voters elected all 28 seats in the Lower House of the 【40†Althing】 and eight of the fourteen seats in Upper House.^{【55†[2]】} The 【43†Citizens' Party】, a loose collection of conservatives,^{【56†[3]】} emerged as the largest party in the Lower House, winning 16 of the 28 seats.
L134: ## Electoral system
L135: 
L136: [【57†edit】]
L137: 
L138: This was the first election held following changes made to the electoral system in 1920, in which two extra seats were allocated to 【58†Reykjavík】. Whilst all seats had previously been elected in one or two-member constituencies, the four-member constituency for Reykjavík was now elected by 【59†proportional representation】 using the 【60†D'Hondt method】.^{【55†[2]】}
L139: The changes also equalised the age limits for voting between men (25) and women and servants (previously 40) at 25.^{【55†[2]】}

L225: Parliamentary elections were held in 【89†Iceland】 on 9 July 1927.[ 1 ] Voters elected all 28 seats in the Lower House of the 【40†Althing】 and eight of the fourteen seats in Upper House.[ 2 ] The 【43†Progressive Party】 emerged as the largest party in the Lower House, winning 13 of the 28 seats.

L124: Elections to the Upper House of the 【39†Althing】 were held in 【45†Iceland】 on 15 June 1930.^{【46†[1]】} Following reforms in 1915, the six seats in the Upper House appointed by the monarch were abolished, and replaced with six elected seats.^{【47†[2]】} The seats were elected by 【48†proportional representation】 at the national level, using the 【49†D'Hondt method】.^{【47†[2]】} The remaining eight seats were elected along with the Lower House.
L125: This was the last election solely for the Upper House, as from 1934 onwards all Upper House members were elected together with the Lower House.^{【47†[2]】}

L133: Parliamentary elections were held in 【50†Iceland】 on 12 June 1931.^{【51†[1]】} Voters elected all 28 seats in the Lower House of the 【41†Althing】 and eight of the fourteen seats in Upper House.^{【52†[2]】} The 【45†Progressive Party】 emerged as the largest party in the Lower House.

L136: Parliamentary elections were held in 【53†Iceland】 on 24 June 1934.^{【54†[1]】} They were the first held after reforms to the electoral system that increased the number of seats in the Lower House from 28 to 33 and ensured that all members of the 【41†Althing】 were elected at the same election. The 【42†Independence Party】 emerged as the largest party in the Lower House, winning 14 of the 33 seats.
L137: ## Electoral reform
L138: 
L139: [【55†edit】]
L140: 
L141: In the previous election, the 28 members of the Lower House 【41†Althing】 had been elected in one- or two-member constituencies by plurality voting, except in 【56†Reykjavík】, where the four seats were elected by proportional representation. Eight members of the Upper House were elected at the same time as the Lower House, whilst the remaining six members were elected in separate national elections using proportional representation.^{【57†[2]】}
L142: The reforms raised the number of seats in the Lower House to 33, of which 11 were to be compensatory seats. The compensatory seats were awarded to parties which had won at least one of the 22 standard seats, and were allocated according to their votes received divided by the seats they had won.^{【58†[3]】} Once allocated to a party, the seats were then allocated based on a preferential basis:^{【58†[3]】}
L143:   1. The party's candidate who had won the highest number of votes in a constituency, but was not elected.
L144:   2. The party's candidate who had won the highest percentage of the votes in a constituency, but was not elected.
L145:   3. The top candidate on a party's nationwide list (if they had used one).
L146:   4. The party's candidate with the second highest number of votes in a constituency, but was not elected.
L147: Although a party could only have one compensatory seat in each constituency, this still left some constituencies over-represented.^{【58†[3]】}
L148: All seats in the Upper House seats were now elected at the same time as the Lower House, whilst the number was increased from 14 to 16.^{【59†[4]】} In Reykjavík the number of seats was increased from four to six, with a subsequent lowering of the threshold to win a seat in the city. The voting age was lowered to 21, and those receiving 【60†poor relief】 were able to vote for the first time.^{【58†[3]】}

L227: Parliamentary elections were held in 【92†Iceland】 on 29 June 1937.[ 1 ] Although the 【41†Independence Party】 won a plurality of votes, the 【43†Progressive Party】 emerged as the largest party in the Lower House of the 【40†Althing】, winning 12 of the 33 seats.

L128: Indirect presidential elections were held in 【55†Iceland】 on 17 June 1944 following the approval of a new constitution and the transition of the country to a republic 【56†the previous month】. 【50†Sveinn Björnsson】 was elected and appointed by the 【49†Parliament】 for a one-year term.^{【57†[1]】}

L139: Parliamentary elections were held in 【56†Iceland】 on 30 June 1946.^{【57†[1]】} The 【47†Independence Party】 remained the largest party in the Lower House of the 【46†Althing】, winning 13 of the 35 seats.^{【58†[2]】}
L140: ## Electoral system
L141: 
L142: [【59†edit】]
L143: The elections were conducted under 【60†rural–urban proportional representation】. Twenty-one members were elected in single-member constituencies via 【61†first-past-the-post voting】, while the remainder were elected using 【62†D'Hondt method】 【63†proportional representation】: twelve members in two-member constituencies, eight members in 【64†Reykjavík】, and eleven from a single national compensatory list. To earn national list seats, a party had to win at least one constituency seat.
L144: In constituencies electing two or more members, within the party list, voters had the option to re-rank the candidates and could also strike a candidate out. Allocation of seats to candidates was done using a system based on the 【65†Borda count】.^{【66†[3]】}

L126: 【44†Ásgeir Ásgeirsson】
L127: Early presidential elections were held for the first time in 【47†Iceland】 on 29 June 1952.^{【48†[1]】} The elections were required following the death of incumbent president 【49†Sveinn Björnsson】 on 25 January. Between his death and the elections, the powers of the presidency were constitutionally vested jointly in 【50†Prime Minister】 【51†Steingrímur Steinþórsson】, 【52†Speaker】 of the 【53†Althing】 【54†Jón Pálmason】 and 【55†President of the Supreme Court】 【56†Jón Ásbjörnsson】.
L128: The result was a victory for 【44†Ásgeir Ásgeirsson】, who received 48% of the vote.^{【57†[2]】} This was the first contested presidential election in the history of 【47†Iceland】.
L129: ## Electoral system
L130: 
L131: [【58†edit】]
L132: 
L133: The President of Iceland is elected in one round by plurality via 【59†first-past-the-post voting】.

L239: Parliamentary elections were held in 【96†Iceland】 on 28 June 1953.[ 1 ] The 【45†Independence Party】 remained the largest party in the Lower House of the 【44†Althing】, winning 14 of the 35 seats.[ 2 ]
L240: ## Electoral system
L241: 
L242: [【97†edit】]
L243: The elections were conducted under 【98†rural–urban proportional representation】. Twenty-one members were elected in single-member constituencies via 【99†first-past-the-post voting】, while the remainder were elected using 【100†D'Hondt method】 【101†proportional representation】: twelve members in two-member constituencies, eight members in 【102†Reykjavík】, and eleven from a single national compensatory list. To earn national list seats, a party had to win at least one constituency seat.
L244: In constituencies electing two or more members, within the party list, voters had the option to re-rank the candidates and could also strike a candidate out. Allocation of seats to candidates was done using a system based on the 【103†Borda count】.[ 3 ]

L129: Presidential elections were held in 【48†Iceland】 on 30 June 1968.^{【49†[1]】} The result was a victory for 【45†Kristján Eldjárn】, who received 66% of the vote.^{【50†[2]】}

L140: Presidential elections were held in 【52†Iceland】 on 29 June 1980.^{【53†[1]】} The result was a victory for 【45†Vigdís Finnbogadóttir】, who received 34% of the vote.^{【54†[2]】} She became the world's first democratically elected female president.^{【55†[3]】}

L125: 【43†Vigdís Finnbogadóttir】
L126: Presidential elections were held in 【45†Iceland】 on 25 June 1988.^{【46†[1]】} The result was a victory for the incumbent president 【43†Vigdís Finnbogadóttir】, who received 95% of the vote.^{【47†[2]】} The election marked the first time an incumbent president was challenged when running for re-election.^{【48†[3]】}
L127: ## Electoral system
L128: 
L129: [【49†edit】]
L130: 
L131: The President of Iceland is elected in one round by 【50†first-past-the-post voting】.

L224: Presidential elections were held in 【90†Iceland】 on 29 June 1996.[ 1 ] The result was a victory for 【45†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】, who received 41.4% of the vote.[ 2 ][ 3 ][ 4 ]
L225: ## Electoral system
L226: 
L227: [【91†edit】]
L228: 
L229: The President of Iceland is elected in one round by 【92†first-past-the-post voting】.
L230: ## Campaign
L231: 
L232: [【93†edit】]
L233: 
L234: Prime minister 【94†Davíð Oddsson】 and former foreign minister 【95†Jón Baldvín Hannibalsson】 considered running in the election.[ 3 ] Guðrún Pétursdóttir, an academic, ran, but withdrew from the race ten days prior to the election date.[ 3 ]
L235: Ólafur was considered a left-wing politician at the time, having been the leader of the left-wing 【96†People's Alliance】 from 1987 to 1995.[ 3 ] 【47†Guðrún Agnarsdóttir】, a former member of parliament for the 【97†Women's List】, was considered on the left as well.[ 3 ] Pétur Hafstein announced his candidacy shortly after Davíð decided not to run.
L236: Pétur was a 【68†Supreme Court】 judge, and was expected to appeal to voters of the conservative 【98†Independence Party】.[ 3 ] Ólafur's campaign was described by political scientist Ólafur Harðarson as "Americanized", as Ólafur emphasized his personal qualities rather than his political background and views.[ 3 ]

L132: Presidential elections were held in 【59†Iceland】 on Saturday, 26 June 2004.
L133: Traditionally, Icelandic presidential elections in which the incumbent president indicates a wish to obtain a new mandate are uncontested. The incumbent 【60†president】, 【57†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】, was first elected in 1996 with 41.4% of the vote,^{【61†[1]】} in an election with an 85.9% turnout contested by four candidates. In 2000 he was re-elected without opposition. When Ólafur Ragnar announced his intention to seek another mandate in 2004, two other candidates emerged:
L134:     【62†Ástþór Magnússon】, a businessman and peace activist, who won 2.6% of the vote in the 1996 election and failed to obtain the necessary 1,500 supporters when he attempted to stand in the 2000 election, and
L135:     【58†Baldur Ágústsson】, a businessman who was essentially unknown to the general public.
L136: Unlike parliamentary elections in Iceland, presidential elections are not fought on the basis of party politics; instead, candidates attempt to use their personalities to attract supporters and appear as a living symbol of national unity.
L137: By tradition, the presidency is an almost entirely powerless office, as the presidents almost never use the powers granted to them by the 【63†constitution】, instead just exercising 【64†moral authority】. Ólafur Ragnar, however, has expressed a wish to have a public discussion on the role of the head of state. Unprecedentedly in the history of the Icelandic Republic, on 2 June 2004 Ólafur Ragnar vetoed a media ownership law passed by the 【65†Althing】.
L138: 【66†Davíð Oddsson】, who was 【67†Prime Minister】 at the time, claimed that the veto was tainted because the president's daughter worked for 【68†Baugur Group】, which had recently acquired roughly half of the country's media. There was little doubt that Ólafur Ragnar would be re-elected, but the veto controversy had an effect on the voting – the unprecedentedly high number of empty ballots (20.6% of the total) was thought to be largely a protest of the veto.
L139: ## Electoral system
L140:

L142: 
L143: The President of Iceland is elected in one round by 【70†first-past-the-post】 voting.

L223: Presidential elections were planned to be held in 【86†Iceland】 on 28 June 2008.[ 1 ]
L224: The incumbent president 【44†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】, 【87†first elected in 1996】, stated in his 【88†New Year】's speech that he would contest the election for a fourth term.[ 2 ]
L225: 
L226: 【89†Ástþór Magnússon】, who ran unsuccessfully in 1996 and 【42†2004】, ruled out running for the presidency.[ 3 ]
L227: 
L228: No challenger to the incumbent president filed by the deadline to declare a candidacy on 24 May 2008,[ 4 ] and so Ólafur Ragnar's fourth term was won uncontested.[ 5 ]
L229: 
L230: Ólafur Ragnar was sworn in on 1 August 2008.[ 6 ]

L139: Elected President
L140: 【58†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】
L141: 
L142: Presidential elections were held in 【61†Iceland】 on 30 June 2012.^{【62†[1]】} The result was a victory for the incumbent 【58†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】, who defeated his nearest rival 【59†Thóra Arnórsdóttir】 by nearly 20% of the vote, and went on to serve a record fifth term as 【63†president of Iceland】.
L143: ## Electoral system
L144: 
L145: [【64†edit】]
L146: 
L147: The President of Iceland is elected in one round by 【65†first-past-the-post voting】.
L148: ## Candidates and campaign
L149: 
L150: [【66†edit】]
L151: 
L152: There were six candidates, but the election became a contest between the incumbent president, and the journalist Thóra Arnórsdóttir, who wanted to return the presidency to a more ceremonial role.
L153: 
L154: Main candidates:
L155:   * The incumbent president, 【58†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】, initially stated he would not seek re-election,^{【67†[2]】}^{【68†[3]】}^{【69†[4]】} but then stated on 4 March that he would run for a fifth term, after receiving a petition of over 30,000 voters in favour of his candidacy.^{【70†[5]】} Speaking in 【71†Selfoss】, he said that "under normal circumstances I would have come to a different conclusion, but more than 30,000 Icelanders, which is a significant part of all the voters in Iceland, requested that I continue.
L156: Many significant matters that are likely to lead to conflict and confrontations are going to be on the agenda in the coming years."^{【72†[6]】}
L157:   * 【59†Thóra Arnórsdóttir】, a journalist and news presenter. She announced her candidacy on 4 April and received the necessary 1,500 signatures in one weekend.
L158: Others:
L159:   * 【60†Ari Trausti Guðmundsson】, a writer, geophysicist and formerly of the 【73†Communist Party of Iceland】, but now an independent.
L160:   * Dr. Herdís Thorgeirsdóttir,^{【74†[7]】} a lawyer and professor of constitutional law and human rights at 【75†Bifröst University】, announced her candidacy on 30 March.^{【76†[8]】} She called a press meeting that day and said her campaign would be an experiment on democracy, whether it was possible to run without the backing of powerful financial actors and political parties.
L161: She referred to the financial collapse in 2008 and the Parliamentary investigative report which concluded that the main reason for the collapse were the close ties between politics and the corporate world seriously damaging the democratic process. Her candidacy was an attempt to increase accountability in the democratic process by not accepting funding from corporations as it is crucial in the struggle against prevailing corruption to limit the influence of money in elections.
L162: She is the President^{【77†[9]】} of the 【78†European Women Women Lawyers' Association】 and Iceland's representative at the 【79†Venice Commission】 of the 【80†Council of Europe】.
L163:   * Andrea Jóhanna Ólafsdóttir, former chairwoman of 【81†Hagsmunasamtök heimilanna】, a 【82†non-governmental organisation】 founded in the wake of the 【83†2008–2012 Icelandic financial crisis】. A vocal critic of both government and financial institutions, she announced her candidacy on 1 May.^{【84†[10]】} She supports the 【85†minimum wage】 of 193,000 krona.
L164:   * Hannes Bjarnason, a farmer who lived in Norway for 14 years. He seeks to enhance the place of "morality" in the public debate and to "safeguard" national interests.
L165: Two other candidates declared their intent to stand in the election, but later dropped out:^{【86†[11]】}
L166: 
L167:   * Jón Lárusson, a police inspector charged with investigating tax fraud since the economic crisis. He claims to be apolitical and has opposed 【87†membership of the EU】.^{【88†[12]】}
L168:   * 【89†Ástþór Magnússon】, previously a candidate in the 【90†2004 election】, a businessman and pacifist, who announced his candidacy on 3 March 2012.^{【91†[13]】}
L169: ## Campaign
L170: 
L171: [【92†edit】]
L172: After trailing in the opinion polls, Ólafur resorted to a 【93†negative campaign】 against Thóra, saying she would be "dangerous for the country" and that she would "do nothing but follow the government's will, particularly in terms of foreign policy", in continuing its membership application to the 【94†European Union】 being pursued by the current government led by 【95†Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir】's 【96†Social Democratic Alliance】, and he had reservations about the prospect of being a member of the EU.
L173: He also accused the Icelandic media of giving Thóra preferential treatment.^{【88†[12]】} Ólafur also claimed to be the best person to steer Iceland through financial crisis.^{【72†[6]】} Thóra also accused Ólafur of distorting the president's role from that of a 【97†figurehead】 to a more political position^{【86†[11]】} and that she would return the post to its ceremonial stature instead of getting involved in politics.^{【98†[14]】} However, Ólafur was said to be popular because of the two referendums Iceland held over the financial crisis and, as a result, many Icelanders felt he was looking out for their interests^{【99†[15]】} after being seen to have stood up to the 【100†United Kingdom】 and the 【101†Netherlands】 over 【102†Icesave】 repayments.^{【103†[16]】}
L174: Thóra told the 【104†Reykjavik Grapevine】 that Iceland needs new leadership: "I think we have all felt a strong need for a change in this country. Iceland is a small country, and we pretty much agree on how this society should be;" she also told 【105†Morgunbladid】 that her lack of experience in politics was not a bad thing as she "think[s] that now is an opportunity to learn from the experience we have been through ...
L175: and use it for a new beginning...[although the presidency is largely ceremonial, the position] has a great power of influence."^{【106†[17]】}
L176: ## Opinion polls
L177: 
L178: [【107†edit】]
L179: 
L180: An 【108†opinion poll】 published on 21 May by the Institute of Social Sciences at the 【109†University of Iceland】 showed Thóra leading with 46.2%, with Ólafur on 37.8%. However, after she suspended her campaign as she was due to give birth, the gap narrowed as Ólafur stood alone as the leading campaigner.^{【88†[12]】} An average of three poll prior to the election indicated Ólafur leading with 45% and Thóra in second place with 37.7% ahead of four other candidates.^{【72†[6]】}

L191: ## Conduct
L192: 
L193: [【118†edit】]
L194: Voting centres were open from 9AM to 10PM. After having voted, Thóra said to 【119†DV】: "You see this glorious day, I can't be anything but optimistic. The 【120†Gallup】 poll gives a strong indication of the outcome, but we will just count the votes and accept whatever that brings us. To have the possibility to topple the current president is a victory in itself." The same day Ólafur wrote in Morgunbladid: "Iceland is now at a crossroads. Behind us are difficult years.
L195: Ahead are decisions on the constitution and our relationship with other countries in Europe. There is still turbulence in the continent's economy and in many areas... The president...shall assist the country in tackling the biggest issues; they will determine the fate of Icelanders for decades."^{【98†[14]】}

L213: ### Reactions
L214: 
L215: [【125†edit】]
L216: 
L217: After partial results were released Thóra told 【126†RUV】: "This has been a valuable experience. Now I will take a holiday, attend to my new daughter and the other children and go on maternity leave and think how I can put this experience to use. To get more than one-third [of votes], I'm overwhelmed. I of course hoped to win. This is something you only do once in a lifetime," as she indicated she would not run in the 【127†next election】.^{【128†[26]】}
L218: ## Analysis
L219: 
L220: [【129†edit】]
L221: 
L222: According to 【130†Euronews】, Ólafur's win was seen as having "emboldened a presidential office that had up until then played a mainly ceremonial role".^{【131†[27]】}
L223: If one of the female candidates had won, Iceland would have had nearly all its leading governing and religious positions held by women; the female president would be 【132†head of state】, 【95†Jóhanna Sigurðardóttir】 would be 【133†head of government】, 【134†Ásta Ragnheiður Jóhannesdóttir】 would be the 【135†Althing】 speaker, while 【136†Agnes M. Sigurðardóttir】 would have been the head of the 【137†Church of Iceland】.^{【88†[12]】}

L147: 
L148: Presidential elections were held in 【67†Iceland】 on 25 June 2016.^{【68†[1]】} President 【66†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】, 【69†elected in 1996】, stepped down after serving five consecutive terms. The history professor 【62†Guðni Th. Jóhannesson】 was elected after receiving a 【70†plurality】 of 39.1% of the vote.^{【71†[2]】} He took office on 1 August, as the first new president of Iceland in twenty years.^{【72†[3]】}
L149: ## Electoral system
L150: 
L151: [【73†edit】]
L152: 
L153: The 【74†President of Iceland】 is elected by 【70†plurality】 in a 【75†single round of voting】.^{【76†[4]】} Candidates must be Icelandic citizens and at least 35 years of age on election day.^{【77†[5]】}
L154: ## Campaign
L155: 
L156: [【78†edit】]
L157: On 1 January 2016 incumbent president 【66†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】 announced that he would not seek a sixth term in the office, wanting "to transfer the responsibilities of the president onto other shoulders".^{【68†[1]】}^{【79†[6]】}^{【80†[7]】} He later retracted and decided to run in April,^{【81†[8]】} citing political unrest after the fallout of the 【82†Panama Papers】 leak, which implicated Prime Minister 【83†Sigmundur Davíð Gunnlaugsson】 and forced him to resign after 【84†large anti-government protests】.^{【85†[9]】} In the following ten days five other candidates suspended their campaigns, one of them after endorsing Ólafur Ragnar.
L158: Former Prime Minister 【65†Davíð Oddsson】 declared his candidacy on 8 May, and Ólafur Ragnar withdrew from the race the following day, stating that there was now a supply of qualified candidates. A poll showing Ólafur Ragnar with only 25% support had been published the same day.^{【86†[10]】}
L159: Davíð Oddsson attacked Guðni Th. Jóhannesson in two TV-debates for allegedly having an unpatriotic view of the 【87†Cod Wars】. Guðni, a historian of the Cod Wars, dismissed these charges and explained that his take on the Cod Wars was nuanced and supported by research. Davíð has also said that Guðni supported Icelandic responsibility for 【88†Icesave】 and is in favor of EU membership.
L160: Guðni responded, saying that his words were taken out context in both instances, and that he as President would make sure that the public would have a say in a referendum both on the resumption of EU accession negotiations and approval of any accession treaty. Furthermore, Davíð has alleged that Guðni will "undermine the Constitution" by supporting constitutional change.^{【89†[11]】} Halla is personally against EU membership and Andri Snær is undecided.
L161: ### End-of-campaign developments
L162: 
L163: [【90†edit】]
L164: Despite an initial anti-establishment feeling, interest in the campaign waned in the last days due to the performance of the 【91†Iceland national football team】 in the 【92†Euro 2016】. Like his predecessor, Guðni is opposed to membership of the 【93†European Union】.
L165: In the final debate the day before the vote, he said the 【94†result of the Brexit vote】 changes "much for the better for us Icelanders", implying that the 【95†European Economic Area】 agreement that non-EU members Norway and Iceland have with the EU could play a more important role with the United Kingdom on board. His campaign promises included vowing to "modernise political life" and give voters a chance of 【96†direct democracy】 initiatives.^{【72†[3]】}
L166: ## Candidates
L167: 
L168: [【97†edit】]
L169: Candidates had to formally declare their intention to run on or before 20 May^{【98†[12]】} (five weeks prior to the election) and "be proposed by not less than 1500 voters".^{【77†[5]】} The number of candidates in previous elections had been six at most, but the announced departure of the incumbent president prompted an unprecedented number of people to consider running. A total of 21 people publicly declared their intention to run, and around ten more were reported to be seriously considering it.
L170: Finally, nine candidates fulfilled the requirements for ballot access.^{【99†[13]】}
L171: ### Elected President
L172: 
L173: [【100†edit】]
L174: 
L175:   * 【62†Guðni Th. Jóhannesson】 – 【101†senior lecturer】 in history at the 【102†University of Iceland】 and author.^{【103†[14]】} He was elected president in the election and served as president from August 1 2016 until August 1 2024.
L176: ### Main candidates
L177: 
L178: [【104†edit】]
L179:   * 【64†Andri Snær Magnason】 – author and environmentalist.^{【105†[15]】}
L180:   * 【65†Davíð Oddsson】 – editor-in-chief of 【106†Morgunblaðið】 and former 【107†Prime Minister】 for the 【108†Independence Party】.^{【109†[16]】}^{【110†[17]】}
L181:   * 【63†Halla Tómasdóttir】 – entrepreneur and investor, co-founder of 【111†Audur Capital】. She was later elected president in 2024 presidential election and is incumbent president of Iceland.^{【112†[18]】}
L182:   * 【113†Sturla Jónsson】 – truck driver, protester, former parliamentary candidate and chairman of the 【114†Sturla Jónsson】 party.^{【115†[19]】}^{【116†[20]】}
L183: ### Other candidates
L184: 
L185: [【117†edit】]
L186:   * 【118†Ástþór Magnússon】 – businessman and 【119†peace activist】; 【120†perennial candidate】, who had previously run for 【74†president】 three times, in 【69†1996】, 【121†2004】, and 【122†2012】.^{【123†[21]】}^{【124†[22]】}^{【125†[23]】} Ran for president one more time in 2024.
L187:   * 【126†Elísabet Jökulsdóttir】 – author and freelance journalist.^{【127†[24]】}
L188:   * Guðrún Margrét Pálsdóttir – nurse and founder of ABC Barnahjálp, an aid organization focusing on children in Asia and Africa.^{【128†[25]】}
L189:   * Hildur Þórðardóttir – 【129†ethnologist】, author, independent publisher and 【130†healer】.^{【131†[26]】}
L190: ### Failed to get ballot access
L191: 
L192: [【132†edit】]
L193: 
L194: Two candidates failed to collect enough signatures before the deadline expired.^{【133†[27]】}^{【134†[28]】}
L195: 
L196:   * 【135†Baldur Ágústsson】 – businessman, who also ran in 【121†2004】.^{【136†[29]】}^{【137†[30]】} Did not submit before the deadline.^{【134†[28]】}
L197:   * Magnús Ingberg Jónsson – fish processing engineer and entrepreneur.^{【138†[31]】} Made an incomplete submission and was rejected by electoral authorities.^{【139†[32]】}
L198: ### Suspended campaign
L199: 
L200: [【140†edit】]
L201:   * Ari Jósepsson – entertainer and self-proclaimed "YouTube star". Declared in January and withdrew on 13 May due to lack of media coverage of minor candidates.^{【141†[33]】}^{【142†[34]】}
L202:   * Benedikt Kristján Mewes – German-born dairy engineer and mailman, who wants to be the first gay president.^{【143†[35]】} Failed to collect enough signatures and withdrew on the last day to hand them in.^{【144†[36]】}
L203:   * Bæring Ólafsson – former COO of 【145†Coca-Cola】 Bottlers Philippines.^{【146†[37]】}^{【147†[38]】} Declared in March and withdrew in late April.^{【148†[39]】} Endorsed Andri Snær Magnason.^{【149†[40]】}
L204:   * Guðmundur Franklín Jónsson – businessman and former chairman of the 【150†Right-Greens】.^{【151†[41]】} Announced in March and left in April. Endorsed Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson.^{【152†[42]】} Ran for president in 2020.
L205:   * Heimir Örn Hólmarsson – 【153†electrical engineer】 and project manager.^{【154†[43]】} Announced in March and withdrew on 19 April due to the incumbent seeking reelection.^{【155†[44]】}
L206:   * Hrannar Pétursson – 【156†sociologist】 and former 【157†Human Resource-】 and Marketing Director for Icelandic 【158†Vodafone】.^{【159†[45]】} Withdrew in April.^{【160†[46]】}
L207:   * Magnus Ingi Magnússon – restaurateur and caterer.^{【161†[47]】} Declared in April, withdrew on 17 May due to lack of signatures, saying he considered running for the Althingi instead.^{【162†[48]】}
L208:   * 【66†Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson】 – Incumbent President. In January, he declared that he would not seek reelection,^{【79†[6]】} but decided to enter the race on 18 April after political unrest in connection with the 【82†Panama Papers】 leak.^{【81†[8]】} He subsequently withdrew on 9 May stating as his reason that other qualified candidates had now entered the race.^{【163†[49]】}
L209:   * Vigfús Bjarni Albertsson – hospital chaplain.^{【164†[50]】} Announced his candidacy in March but withdrew on 18 April.^{【165†[51]】}
L210:   * 【166†Þorgrímur Þráinsson】 – author, motivational speaker, and former 【167†football】 player; announced he intended to run in November 2015,^{【168†[52]】}^{【169†[53]】}^{【170†[54]】} which he confirmed on 1 January.^{【127†[24]】} In April however, he said he would not go forth and implied he had not made a declaration.^{【171†[55]】}
L211: ### Declined
L212: 
L213: [【172†edit】]
L214: 
L215:   * 【173†Baldur Thorhallsson】 – Professor of Political Science at the University of Iceland.^{【174†[56]】}^{【175†[57]】}^{【176†[58]】} Ran for president in 2024.
L216:   * 【177†Jón Gnarr】 – comedian and former 【178†Mayor of Reykjavík】^{【179†[59]】} Ran for president in 2024.
L217:   * 【180†Katrín Jakobsdóttir】 – leader of the 【181†Left-Green Movement】^{【182†[60]】} Ran for president in 2024.

L221:

L247: ## Results
L248: 
L249: [【205†edit】]
L250: 
L251: Guðni won the election with 39.1% of the votes.^{【71†[2]】} Halla received 27.9%, Andri Snær 14.3%, Davíð 13.7% and Sturla 3.5%.^{【71†[2]】} The turnout was 75.7%.^{【71†[2]】}
L252: 
L253: After voting on his birthday, Guðni said that he was satisfied he had "managed to present to the people my vision of the presidency." He said that should he win, he would first "go to France on Monday and see 【206†Iceland play England】."^{【72†[3]】}

L137: Presidential elections were held in 【56†Iceland】 on 27 June 2020.^{【57†[1]】} Absentee voting opened on 25 May 2020.^{【58†[2]】} Incumbent president 【54†Guðni Th. Jóhannesson】 was re-elected with 92% of the vote.
L138: ## Electoral system
L139: 
L140: [【59†edit】]
L141: 
L142: The 【60†President of Iceland】 is elected by 【61†first-past-the-post voting】,^{【62†[3]】} with a simple 【63†plurality】 of votes needed to win.
L143: ## Candidates
L144: 
L145: [【64†edit】]
L146: 
L147: Incumbent 【60†president of Iceland】 【54†Guðni Th. Jóhannesson】 announced in his new year's address on 1 January 2020 that he would seek re-election.^{【65†[4]】}
L148: 
L149: 【55†Guðmundur Franklín Jónsson】, a businessman and activist, announced that he would run for the office of president in a Facebook-live video on 22 April.^{【66†[5]】}
L150: Several other persons announced their interest in running for the office, including Axel Pétur Axelsson, a self described social engineer, who was quoted as saying that his first matter of business as president would be to dismiss all members of the Icelandic government.^{【67†[6]】} Only the incumbent president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson and challenger Guðmundur Franklín Jónsson gathered the required number of signatures to get on the ballot.^{【68†[7]】}

L122: Parliamentary elections were held in 【46†Iceland】 on 5 August 1916,^{【47†[1]】} the first elections held after 【48†women's suffrage】 was introduced.^{【49†[2]】} Following reforms to the 【37†Althing】 the previous year, the six seats in the Upper House appointed by the monarch were abolished, and replaced with six elected seats.^{【49†[2]】} The seats were elected by 【50†proportional representation】 at the national level, using the 【51†D'Hondt method】.^{【49†[2]】} The remaining eight seats were elected along with the Lower House 【52†in October】.

L134: Parliamentary elections were held in 【50†Iceland】 on 5 July 1942.^{【51†[1]】} Although the 【41†Independence Party】 won a plurality of votes, the 【43†Progressive Party】 remained as the largest party in the Lower House of the 【40†Althing】, winning 14 of the 33 seats.
L135: 
L136: Following the election, changes were made to the electoral system that reduced the over-representation of the Progressive Party.^{【52†[2]】} 【53†Early elections】 were held in October.

L137: Parliamentary elections were held in 【54†Iceland】 on 28 June 1959.^{【55†[1]】} The 【45†Independence Party】 and the 【47†Progressive Party】 both won 13 seats in the Lower House of the 【44†Althing】.^{【56†[2]】} Following the tie, electoral reforms were introduced and 【57†early elections】 were held in October.
L138: ## Electoral system
L139: 
L140: [【58†edit】]
L141: The elections were conducted under 【59†rural–urban proportional representation】. Twenty-one members were elected in single-member constituencies via 【60†first-past-the-post voting】, while the remainder were elected using 【61†D'Hondt method】 【62†proportional representation】: twelve members in two-member constituencies, eight members in 【63†Reykjavík】, and eleven from a single national compensatory list. To earn national list seats, a party had to win at least one constituency seat.
L142: In constituencies electing two or more members, within the party list, voters had the option to re-rank the candidates and could also strike a candidate out. Allocation of seats to candidates was done using a system based on the 【64†Borda count】.^{【65†[3]】}

L139: Parliamentary elections were held in 【51†Iceland】 on 21 October 1916.[ 1 ] Voters elected all 26 seats in the Lower House of the 【52†Althing】 and eight of the fourteen seats in Upper House,[ 2 ] the other six having been 【35†elected in August】. The 【37†Home Rule Party】 emerged as the largest party in the Lower House of the 【52†Althing】, winning eight of the 26 seats.

L225: Early parliamentary elections were held in 【89†Iceland】 on 18 and 19 October 1942.[ 1 ] They were held after reforms were made to the electoral system following the 【38†July elections】. The 【41†Independence Party】 emerged as the largest party in the Lower House of the 【40†Althing】, winning 13 of the 35 seats.
L226: ## Electoral reform
L227: 
L228: [【90†edit】]
L229: In the previous two elections in 【91†1937】 and July 1942 the Independence Party had received the most votes, yet had received fewer seats than the 【43†Progressive Party】, which had received more than 10% less of the vote.[ 2 ] However, following the July election, changes were made to the electoral system that reduced the over-representation of the Progressive Party.[ 3 ] This involved introducing 【92†proportional representation】 to the two six-member constituencies and increasing the number of seats in 【93†Reykjavík】 where PR was already in use, lowering its effective threshold from 11.3% to 8.7%.[ 3 ]
L230: Whilst both parties received a similar number of votes as in July (the IP increased their vote tally by just 26, whilst the PP lost 164 votes), the Independence Party won two extra seats in the Lower House, whilst the Progressive Party lost four.[ 2 ]

L137: Early parliamentary elections were held in 【54†Iceland】 on 25 and 26 October 1959.^{【55†[1]】} Following the electoral reforms made after the 【56†June elections】, the 【45†Independence Party】 won 16 of the 40 seats in the Lower House of the 【44†Althing】.^{【57†[2]】}
L138: ## Electoral reforms
L139: 
L140: [【58†edit】]
L141: The June 1959 elections had ended with both the Independence Party and the 【47†Progressive Party】 winning 13 seats, despite the IP receiving 42% of the vote to the PP's 27%.^{【59†[3]】} The electoral system at the time was 【60†rural–urban proportional representation】: a lower tier comprised single member 【61†constituencies】 elected using 【62†first-past-the-post voting】, two-member constituencies elected using 【63†party-list proportional representation】 (party-list PR) and one large multi-member constituency for 【64†Reykjavík】 that also used party-list PR, topped up by an upper tier of eleven seats chosen from a single national compensatory list.^{【65†[4]】}^{【66†[5]】}
L142: The reforms saw the replacement of this rural-urban proportional system with a two-tier party-list PR system; the lower tier now comprised eight multi-member constituencies, all elected using party-list PR.^{【66†[5]】}^{【65†[4]】} Five constituencies elected five members each, two elected six members each and Reykjavík elected 12.
L143: The number of seats for Reykjavík was also increased from the prior elections,^{【66†[5]】} increasing the overall total in the Lower House from 35 to 40 and in the Upper House from 17 to 20.^{【67†[6]】}
L144: The voters’ capacity to change the order of names on the PR lists was greatly reduced compared to prior elections as well; the existing 【68†Borda count】-based system was now only being used to calculate one-third of the final number of votes deemed to have been received by each candidate, while the party’s unaltered ordering determined the remaining two-thirds.^{【65†[4]】}
